en.title: Rethinking GraphQL - 05: The Evolution of Web Architecture—How Does RSC Change GraphQL’s Value?
en.subtitle: From Facebook’s design philosophy to the engineering challenges of real-world adoption

text.text: From CSR and SSR to RSC: how do frontend and backend responsibilities change?
RSC’s central change: components can access server-side data directly.
RSC and Relay: two ways to organize data dependencies.
Server Components do not automatically solve N+1 or caching problems.
GraphQL @defer, @stream, and React Suspense: incremental data delivery and progressive rendering.
RSC’s limits: which problems still need APIs and client data management?
GraphQL’s new position in modern web architecture.
This chapter asks how GraphQL’s technical role should be reassessed as web applications change how they fetch data and render content.

Previous chapters examined GraphQL within Facebook’s systems and its engineering challenges in wider adoption. Evaluating it also requires considering another variable: web application architecture itself is changing.

GraphQL originated in 2012, as Facebook moved its mobile applications from HTML5 to native implementations. Clients needed structured data to build their own interfaces. The subsequent spread of React and other frontend frameworks reinforced a model in which clients rendered the UI and servers supplied data through APIs.

React Server Components (RSC) rearrange that division. Some React components can execute directly on the server, fetch data from databases or business services, and send their rendered output to clients.
Data that previously had to reach the browser through GraphQL or REST can, in some architectures, be fetched and consumed directly by Server Components.
This does not mean RSC replaces GraphQL, but it changes some use cases and offers a new perspective on client data management frameworks.
1. From CSR and SSR to RSC: Changing Responsibilities
Understanding RSC’s effect on GraphQL first requires distinguishing three technologies:
CSR: Client-Side Rendering.
SSR: Server-Side Rendering.
RSC: React Server Components.

They are often discussed together but address different questions. CSR and SSR mainly concern where pages are generated. RSC additionally concerns where components execute and which implementation code must reach the browser.
1.1 CSR: The Browser Builds the Page
CSR is common in React single-page applications.
Typically, the server returns basic HTML (HyperText Markup Language) and JavaScript assets. The browser downloads and executes JavaScript, and React creates and updates the page.
Business data is generally fetched through an API (Application Programming Interface), such as REST or GraphQL.
A typical flow is:

Browser requests a page
       ↓
Server returns HTML and JavaScript
       ↓
Browser executes React
       ↓
REST / GraphQL retrieves business data
       ↓
React builds and updates the page
Real applications can preload or request data in parallel; the steps need not run strictly in sequence.
React components mainly run in the browser here, while GraphQL can handle browser-to-server queries.
Relay adds management of component requirements, query composition, client caching, and updates.
One CSR limitation is that a complete initial page may wait for JavaScript downloads, execution, and data retrieval. In complex applications this can slow the initial display.
1.2 SSR: The Server Generates HTML First
SSR moves initial HTML generation to the server.
For a post page, the server can fetch the post and author, run React’s server renderer, and generate HTML containing the content.
The browser can display this HTML before JavaScript finishes loading.
A typical flow is:

Browser requests a page
       ↓
Server fetches business data
       ↓
Server runs React to generate HTML
       ↓
Browser receives and displays HTML
       ↓
Browser loads JavaScript
       ↓
React hydrates the page

Hydration means that React establishes its client-side runtime state around existing server-generated HTML and takes control of interactive UI, allowing buttons, inputs, and similar elements to respond to users.
An important distinction is that although SSR generates initial HTML on the server, many components in traditional SSR applications still execute in the browser.
A post component with a like button can generate HTML on the server, then load JavaScript in the browser to provide interaction.
SSR also does not require GraphQL or REST for data access. The server can query databases or internal services directly.
Direct server-side fetching was therefore possible before RSC.
1.3 RSC: Explicit Server and Client Component Boundaries
RSC stands for React Server Components.
It goes beyond deciding where initial HTML is generated by letting developers distinguish two kinds of component:
Server Components execute only on the server. They can access server-side functions, databases, and internal services directly, without sending their implementation code to the browser.
Client Components support client state, event handling, and browser interaction. Their JavaScript must execute in the browser.
A post page might contain:
PostContent: a Server Component that fetches and displays the post body.
LikeButton: a Client Component that handles clicks and interactive state.
The Server Component can call a data access function directly instead of having the browser query GraphQL for post data and then render it.
The like button can remain a Client Component handling interaction.
The key change is an explicit, component-level division of server and browser responsibilities.
Server Component output is not simply ordinary HTML, however.
React produces a transport representation of the rendered Server Components called the React Server Component Payload, commonly shortened to RSC Payload.
It contains rendered results, Client Component references, and associated data, letting React reconstruct or update the component tree on the client.
It is neither complete HTML directly nor simply GraphQL JSON replaced by another JSON response.
1.4 RSC and SSR Can Work Together
SSR and RSC are not mutually exclusive.
They commonly work together in the Next.js App Router.
On initial load, the server can execute Server Components to obtain an RSC Payload, then use SSR to generate initial HTML for a quick first display.
The browser subsequently loads the JavaScript needed to hydrate Client Components. Server Components themselves do not re-execute or hydrate in the browser.
During internal navigation, the client can request a new RSC Payload and update the tree without reloading the entire HTML document.
The distinction is:
SSR concerns generating initial HTML on the server.
RSC concerns component execution boundaries and transporting server-rendered component results to the client.
They can cooperate but are different mechanisms.
2. RSC’s Central Change: Direct Access to Server-Side Data
Consider a React page displaying a post and its author.
In a typical client-side GraphQL architecture, the browser sends a query and gives the returned data to React for rendering.
The basic flow is:

React in the browser
        ↓
   GraphQL query
        ↓
   GraphQL server
        ↓
   Business services / database
        ↓
   JSON returns to the browser
        ↓
   React renders components
With RSC, a post component running on the server can call data access functions during execution.
Those functions can access databases and ORMs or call existing REST, GraphQL, or other internal services.
For example:
getPost can encapsulate server-side data access without corresponding to a dedicated browser-facing HTTP API.
The server sends the component’s rendered output without shipping its data access logic or entire implementation to the browser.
The browser receives the output of React’s server rendering system rather than necessarily consuming GraphQL JSON and turning it into UI itself.
The important change is more than avoiding an HTTP request: some fetching and consumption move inside the server.
If the application server can directly access the database, a REST or GraphQL API whose sole purpose is supplying that browser UI may become unnecessary.
This depends on architecture. If the React server and business backend are independently deployed, or data comes from another company’s services, RSC still needs network APIs.
RSC can remove some browser-facing data APIs, but does not eliminate server-to-server interfaces or the independent value of GraphQL and REST.
3. RSC and Relay: Two Approaches to Data Dependencies
Chapter 2 examined Relay’s fragment colocation.
Components declare requirements, and GraphQL fragments plus a compiler compose them into executable queries. The focus is organizing, reusing, and centrally managing client component dependencies.
RSC also supports component-level data organization, but differently: a Server Component calls a data function directly, potentially defined nearby.
A post component fetches the post, a comments component fetches comments, and an author component fetches the author.
These components execute server functions directly. They no longer need GraphQL fragments to declare requirements or a compiler to combine the entire component tree’s needs into one query.
Some engineering goals overlap:
Both aim for clear component dependencies and less centralized management of all requirements in parent components.
Relay coordinates dependencies through static declarations, a compiler, and a client runtime.
RSC gives components server-side execution so they can fetch data while running.
There is an important difference.
Relay Compiler analyzes static fragments, generates query structures, and checks them against the schema.
RSC does not require a unified GraphQL schema for dependencies. Components can call arbitrary server functions, leaving optimization and type checking to the chosen access layer and tooling.
RSC reduces dependence on a client-side GraphQL querying layer without automatically supplying all of Relay’s compile-time analysis or caching.
Relay does not become useless because RSC exists.
Applications with substantial browser-side business logic and ongoing server-data fetching and updates can still benefit from Relay’s cache, fragment subscriptions, pagination, and updates.
The central distinctions are where components run and who fetches and maintains their data.
4. Server Components Do Not Automatically Solve N+1 or Caching
Direct server-side access does not make database queries inherently efficient.
A list of 20 post components, each separately loading its author, can still create many repeated database accesses.
This has the same underlying problem as GraphQL resolver N+1: independent requirements are not effectively combined or reused.

Moving components to the server cannot automatically optimize every query into one database operation. Batching, eager loading, joins, request-scoped caching, and other access optimizations remain necessary.

React and Next.js provide some assistance. React’s cache can reuse a data function’s results within one server request. Next.js also provides fetching caches, deduplication, and mechanisms for caching and revalidating different data.
Three distinctions matter:
Deduplication is not batching. A request cache can avoid repeating the same user lookup, but 20 different users do not automatically become one database query.
Caching is not cache consistency. Avatar changes, post edits, and new comments still require policies determining what to invalidate and which components to update.

Server caching is not client normalization. RSC-related server caches mainly reuse fetched data and rendered output. Relay and Apollo manage shared entities, subscriptions, and updates across browser components and queries.
Their implementation layers and goals differ.
RSC moves some caching concerns without eliminating the complexity of loading, caching, and consistency.
That is one reason it should not be mistaken for complete backend data infrastructure.
5. GraphQL @defer, @stream, and Suspense: Incremental Data and Progressive Rendering
Different data can take very different amounts of time to retrieve. Waiting for all of it can hold back content that is already ready.
A post page might fetch its body in 100 milliseconds, while recommendations take two seconds because of additional computation and queries.

A conventional GraphQL query requesting both generally waits for execution to complete before returning the full result. The body may be ready much earlier, but reach the client only after two seconds.
One solution is separate requests for the post and recommendations, which is possible with REST or GraphQL.
Another is to return ready data first within the same query, followed by the remaining results.
GraphQL’s @defer and @stream address this incremental-delivery requirement.
5.1 @defer: Returning Query Results in Parts
@defer is an incremental-delivery directive that delays part of a query’s data without waiting for the whole query to finish.
A client can request post content and recommendations, marking recommendations for deferred delivery:
With compatible server and client implementations, execution can proceed as follows:
First, the server retrieves the title and body and delivers them after roughly 100 milliseconds.
It continues processing recommendations and delivers them in an incremental response for the same query after roughly two seconds.
The client can use the received post content before all data is ready.
The key is that @defer controls delivery of query results, not React component rendering.
It allows data to arrive in parts without dictating how the interface displays them.
5.2 @stream: Delivering List Elements Gradually
@stream is also an incremental-delivery directive, primarily for lists.
If a post has 100 comments, the server need not wait until all comments are ready before returning the list.
The client can request an initial subset:
A supporting implementation can deliver the first three comments and progressively deliver the rest.
The main distinction is:
@defer delays a fragment of query data.
@stream delivers list elements incrementally.
Both operate at GraphQL’s data-delivery layer.
Related specifications and implementation support still vary. It cannot be assumed that every server, client, and transport supports these directives.
5.3 Suspense: Rendering While Asynchronous Data Is Pending
Incremental delivery explains how data arrives in parts. How should the UI handle receiving only some of it?
For example, the post is available while recommendations are still loading.
We want to display the post immediately, show a loading state for recommendations, and update that component when its data is ready.
React Suspense can coordinate that behavior.
For example:

Loading recommendations...

}>
If Recommendations depends on a pending asynchronous resource and its data-fetching mechanism supports Suspense, React can temporarily show the fallback.
Once the data is ready, React renders the actual component.
Suspense coordinates rendering while components wait for asynchronous dependencies.
It neither sends @defer instructions nor automatically turns ordinary asynchronous requests into incremental responses. The mechanisms operate at different layers:
GraphQL controls how data returns; Suspense controls how components depending on it are presented.
They can cooperate. Relay can receive incrementally delivered @defer data, write it into its store, and let components read it while using Suspense for unavailable dependencies.
Incremental data delivery and progressive component presentation then work together.
5.4 React Streaming: Progressively Delivering Server-Rendered Output
So far we have discussed query results arriving in parts and components waiting for them.
For server-rendered pages, another question arises: must the server finish the entire page before sending HTML?
Streaming SSR allows completed HTML to be sent first, followed by other rendered parts.
The post body may be rendered while recommendations still await data.
The server can send the post and a recommendations loading state first, then deliver the actual recommendations later.
React Streaming and GraphQL incremental delivery both let clients receive content progressively, but deliver different things:
GraphQL incrementally delivers query data; Streaming SSR incrementally delivers rendered page content.
They can work independently or together in a suitable architecture.
5.5 How Does RSC Relate to These Mechanisms?
RSC additionally lets some React components execute on the server and access its data layer.
Post and recommendations components can both fetch their data as Server Components.
React can combine Suspense and streaming to send completed portions before other Server Component results.
The client may progressively receive an RSC Payload rather than business data returned by a GraphQL query.
RSC determines where components execute, Suspense coordinates asynchronous rendering, and streaming concerns how output is transmitted progressively.
They are different mechanisms. Traditional SSR can also use Suspense and streaming without RSC.
Server Components consume data directly and produce rendered output, so browsers need not first fetch business data through GraphQL or REST and render it themselves.
A Server Component can nevertheless call an independent GraphQL service. RSC does not eliminate every need for data-querying interfaces.
5.6 There Is No Simple Replacement Relationship
Their responsibilities can be summarized as follows:

cells.text: Deferring part of a query’s data
Presenting components while asynchronous dependencies are pending
Server execution boundaries and delivery of Server Component results

text.text: GraphQL incremental delivery and React streaming can produce similar experiences: a page appears progressively without waiting for everything.
They address different layers, however.
Showing different page regions at different times is also not exclusive to GraphQL or RSC.
A REST client can request the post and recommendations in parallel. React displays the body when its response arrives, then updates recommendations later.
Incremental GraphQL support does not automatically confer superior rendering capabilities over REST, and RSC streaming does not directly replace @defer or @stream.
GraphQL describes incremental requirements within structured queries; React coordinates components around asynchronous dependencies; RSC additionally changes where execution and consumption happen.
They can cooperate while retaining independent technical value.
6. BFF, tRPC, and oRPC: Other Ways to Improve API Collaboration
One GraphQL benefit is letting clients request what they need while sharing a typed schema contract with servers.
Other technologies can address these needs too.
Full-stack frameworks, TypeScript, and API tooling offer more approaches to frontend–backend interaction. BFF, tRPC, and oRPC illustrate different ones.
They are not three competing products at the same layer as GraphQL. BFF is an architectural pattern; tRPC and oRPC are primarily tools for building typed APIs.
6.1 BFF: Adapting Data to Each Client on the Server
Backend for Frontend (BFF) supplies dedicated backend interfaces for particular clients.
A company’s web, iOS, and Android clients may all display posts but require different structures.
A conventional approach exposes underlying APIs, leaving clients to fetch posts, authors, and comments and combine them.
A BFF adds a dedicated service between clients and underlying business services.
The web BFF can aggregate posts, authors, and recommendations into one web-specific response. A mobile BFF can provide different structures suited to mobile screens.
Clients need less knowledge of underlying services and do less composition themselves.
GraphQL also retrieves related data, but the approaches differ.
A BFF normally exposes interfaces designed in advance for a client category. GraphQL lets clients choose and compose fields within its schema.
The former places more adaptation logic on the server; the latter gives clients greater query flexibility.
They are not mutually exclusive: a BFF can expose a GraphQL API.
BFF therefore is not a direct GraphQL replacement. It demonstrates that organizing data around client needs does not necessarily require GraphQL.
6.2 tRPC: End-to-End Type Safety Through TypeScript
tRPC, or TypeScript Remote Procedure Call, takes another approach.
GraphQL defines API types through an independent schema. Clients write queries against it and may generate type information through tooling.
tRPC uses TypeScript inference to expose server API types directly to the client.
For example, a server defines a procedure for retrieving a post:
getPost({ id: 100 })
Calling it on the client lets development tools infer argument and return types from the server definition without maintaining a separate GraphQL schema.
This suits TypeScript applications maintained by one team or closely collaborating frontend and backend teams.
Its interface model nevertheless resembles Remote Procedure Call (RPC).
Clients invoke predefined server procedures rather than selecting fields and relationships freely within GraphQL’s shared type system.
The server procedure normally decides what getPost returns. Different combinations may require modifying it or defining additional procedures.
GraphQL lets clients choose different fields from one schema through different queries.
These are different contract designs, not a simple ranking.
tRPC reduces coordination through shared TypeScript types; GraphQL offers composable access through a programming-language-independent schema and query language.
6.3 oRPC: Typed RPC and Standard API Descriptions
oRPC also uses TypeScript for typed remote calls, with runtime input validation and OpenAPI integration.
The OpenAPI Specification describes HTTP APIs in machine-readable form, including paths, parameters, requests, and responses.
Developers can combine TypeScript inference with OpenAPI descriptions for documentation generation and tooling-based integration from other languages.
Its difference from GraphQL remains the underlying API abstraction.
oRPC organizes interfaces around server-defined procedures and their input/output types.
GraphQL provides a query language for objects and relationships in which clients choose their required fields.
oRPC demonstrates that typed, validated APIs with standard descriptions can be built without a GraphQL schema.
An OpenAPI description is nevertheless different from GraphQL field selection and relationship querying.
6.4 Where Does GraphQL’s Competitive Advantage Lie?
BFF, tRPC, and oRPC show that several once-prominent GraphQL benefits now have multiple implementation paths.
A BFF can reduce client requests through aggregation.
TypeScript inference, OpenAPI, and code generation can provide frontend–backend type safety.
Dedicated REST or RPC interfaces can also spare clients from combining multiple underlying services manually.
These capabilities should not be treated as GraphQL-exclusive.
Its more distinctive design combines a common typed data model with structured queries written by clients.

Clients select fields, follow related objects, and compose reusable requirements through fragments within the server’s schema. That freedom also brings execution, authorization, caching, and governance requirements.

Choosing an API therefore requires more than comparing type safety or HTTP request counts. Does the application genuinely need client-driven composition, and is that flexibility worth its engineering cost?
7. GraphQL’s New Position in Modern Web Architecture
The move from client rendering to RSC, together with BFFs and typed RPC, offers different paths for many problems GraphQL originally addressed.
No single technology entirely replaces GraphQL; its necessity varies across architectures.

In tightly integrated full-stack React applications, Server Components can call server data functions directly. If requirements are simple or the backend mainly serves one web client, an extra GraphQL layer may add insufficient value.
For integrated TypeScript projects, tRPC or oRPC may satisfy type safety and collaboration more directly.
Complex client applications can still benefit from structured queries, fragments, and tools such as Relay to manage dependencies across components.
Systems serving web, mobile, third-party apps, and multiple business systems can retain GraphQL as a UI-framework-independent interface.
Multiple clients alone do not justify GraphQL. They must genuinely need flexible selection and composition, and the shared schema must reduce long-term coordination costs.
Its modern roles can be summarized in three scenarios:

cells.text: A browser data interface used with Relay, Apollo, or similar tools
An optional server-side query layer that may be replaced by direct server-function calls
Multi-client platform with complex business data
A common cross-client query contract for composing different requirements

text.text: These scenarios overlap. One system can use RSC, GraphQL, REST, and RPC for different responsibilities.
Modern architecture does not make GraphQL technically obsolete. It removes some fetching tasks previously handled through client APIs.
Its value must be judged in context: do the common schema, structured queries, and composable contract deliver benefits exceeding execution, maintenance, and governance costs?
That provides a foundation for the final chapter’s reassessment of GraphQL’s strengths, limits, and suitable conditions.

text.text: 从 CSR、SSR 到 RSC：前后端职责如何变化？
RSC 的核心变化：组件可以直接访问服务端数据层
RSC 与 Relay：两种不同的数据依赖组织方式
服务端组件并不会自动解决 N+1 与缓存问题
GraphQL
@defer
@stream
与 React Suspense：数据的增量交付与界面的渐进渲染
RSC 的适用边界：哪些问题仍然需要 API 和客户端数据管理？
GraphQL 在现代 Web 架构中的新位置
本章回答：当 Web 应用的数据获取与渲染方式发生变化，GraphQL 的技术价值如何重新定位？
前面几章讨论了 GraphQL 在 Facebook 的技术体系，以及它在行业实践中面临的工程问题。但评价 GraphQL，还需要考虑一个新的变量：Web 应用的架构本身正在发生变化。
GraphQL 诞生于 2012 年。当时，Facebook 正在将移动应用从 HTML5 转向原生实现，客户端需要直接获取结构化数据，再自行构建界面。此后，React 等前端框架的普及，进一步推动了客户端负责 UI 渲染、服务器通过 API 提供数据的开发模式。
然而，React Server Components（RSC）重新调整了这种分工。部分 React 组件现在可以直接在服务器执行，从数据库或业务服务获取数据，并将渲染结果传递给客户端。
这意味着，原本需要通过 GraphQL 或 REST API 交付给浏览器的数据，在某些架构中可以直接由服务端组件获取和消费。
这种变化并不意味着 GraphQL 将被 RSC 替代，但它确实改变了 GraphQL 的部分使用场景，也为重新评价客户端数据管理框架提供了新的视角。
一、从 CSR、SSR 到 RSC：前后端职责如何变化？
理解 React Server Components 对 GraphQL 的影响，首先需要区分三种技术：
CSR（Client-Side Rendering，客户端渲染）
SSR（Server-Side Rendering，服务端渲染）
RSC（React Server Components，React 服务器组件）
这三者经常被放在一起讨论，但解决的问题并不完全相同。CSR 和 SSR 主要涉及页面在哪里生成，RSC 则进一步涉及 React 组件在哪里执行，以及哪些组件代码需要交付给浏览器。
1. CSR：浏览器负责构建页面
CSR 是 React 单页应用中常见的渲染模式。
在典型的 CSR 应用中，服务器先向浏览器返回基础 HTML（HyperText Markup Language，超文本标记语言）和 JavaScript 资源。浏览器下载并执行 JavaScript，由 React 创建和更新页面内容。
业务数据通常通过 API（Application Programming Interface，应用程序编程接口）获取，例如 REST 或 GraphQL。
典型过程如下：

浏览器请求页面
       ↓
服务器返回 HTML 和 JavaScript
       ↓
浏览器执行 React
       ↓
通过 REST / GraphQL 获取业务数据
       ↓
React 根据数据构建和更新页面
实际应用可以提前获取或并行请求数据，并不一定严格按照上述步骤串行执行。
在这种架构中，React 组件主要运行于浏览器，GraphQL 则可以负责浏览器与服务器之间的数据查询。
Relay 在此基础上，进一步管理 React 组件的数据需求、GraphQL 查询组合、客户端缓存和数据更新。
CSR 的主要问题之一是，首次显示完整页面可能需要等待 JavaScript 下载、执行及业务数据获取。对于复杂应用，这些过程可能影响首屏加载速度。
2. SSR：服务器先生成 HTML
SSR 将页面初始 HTML 的生成过程转移到服务器。
例如，用户访问一条帖子页面，服务器可以先获取帖子和作者信息，再运行 React 的服务端渲染过程，生成包含帖子内容的 HTML。
浏览器收到 HTML 后，即使 JavaScript 尚未完成加载，也能够先显示相应内容。
典型过程如下：

浏览器请求页面
       ↓
服务器获取业务数据
       ↓
服务器运行 React，生成 HTML
       ↓
浏览器接收并显示 HTML
       ↓
浏览器加载 JavaScript
       ↓
React 完成 Hydration（注水）
Hydration（注水，也常译为水合）指的是：浏览器已经拥有服务端生成的 HTML，React 随后在客户端建立相应的运行状态，并接管需要交互的界面，使按钮、输入框等能够正常响应用户操作。
这里有一个重要区别：
SSR 虽然在服务器生成初始 HTML，但传统 SSR 应用中的许多 React 组件仍然需要在浏览器执行。
例如，一个具有点赞按钮的帖子组件，可以先在服务器生成 HTML，再由浏览器加载相应 JavaScript，完成客户端交互。
另外，SSR 并不要求服务器必须通过 GraphQL 或 REST 获取数据。服务器完全可以直接访问数据库或内部业务服务。
因此，服务器直接获取数据，并不是后来 RSC 才首次实现的能力。
3. RSC：进一步区分服务器组件与客户端组件
RSC 是 React Server Components，即 React 服务器组件。
与 SSR 不同，RSC 不只是决定在哪里生成初始 HTML，而是允许开发者将 React 组件划分为两类：
Server Components（服务器组件）
：只在服务器执行，可以直接访问服务端数据函数、数据库或内部服务，其组件实现代码不需要发送到浏览器。
Client Components（客户端组件）
：支持客户端状态、事件处理和浏览器交互，其相关 JavaScript 需要在浏览器执行。
例如，一个帖子页面可以包含：
PostContent
：服务器组件，负责获取和展示帖子正文。
LikeButton
：客户端组件，负责响应用户点击、维护交互状态。
在这种架构中，帖子正文可以由服务器组件直接调用数据访问函数获取，而不必让浏览器先向 GraphQL API 请求帖子数据，再自行完成渲染。
另一方面，点赞按钮仍然可以作为客户端组件，负责用户交互。
RSC 的重要变化，是让 React 应用能够在组件层面明确划分服务器和浏览器的职责。
但服务器组件的输出也不只是普通 HTML。
React 会生成一种专门用于表示服务器组件渲染结果的传输数据，称为
React Server Component Payload（React 服务器组件载荷，通常简称 RSC Payload）
这种载荷包含服务器组件的渲染结果、客户端组件的引用以及相关数据，使 React 能够在客户端重建或更新相应的组件树。
它不是直接返回完整 HTML，也不是简单地把 GraphQL JSON 换成另一种 JSON。
4. RSC 与 SSR 可以同时使用
SSR 和 RSC 并不是互斥的两种技术。
以 Next.js App Router（Next.js 应用路由器）为例，两者通常配合使用。
首次打开页面时，服务器可以先执行 Server Components，获得 RSC Payload，再结合 SSR 生成初始 HTML，让浏览器尽快显示页面。
浏览器随后加载需要的 JavaScript，为 Client Components 完成 Hydration。Server Components 本身不需要在浏览器重新执行或注水。
而当用户在应用内部导航时，客户端也可以请求新的 RSC Payload，用于更新 React 组件树，而不必每次重新加载整个 HTML 页面。
因此，需要明确区分：
SSR 关注初始页面如何在服务器生成 HTML。
RSC 关注 React 组件的服务器执行边界，以及服务器组件的结果如何传递给客户端。
两者可以协同工作，但不是同一种机制。
二、RSC 的核心变化：组件可以直接访问服务端数据层
考虑一个展示帖子及作者信息的 React 页面。
在典型的客户端 GraphQL 架构中，浏览器需要向 GraphQL 服务端发送查询，然后将返回数据交给 React 组件渲染。
其基本过程是：

浏览器中的 React
        ↓
   GraphQL 查询
        ↓
  GraphQL 服务端
        ↓
  业务服务 / 数据库
        ↓
 JSON 数据返回浏览器
        ↓
  React 渲染组件
在使用 RSC 的应用中，如果帖子组件本身运行在服务器，就可以在组件执行时直接调用数据访问函数。
这些函数可以访问数据库、ORM，也可以调用已有的 REST、GraphQL 或其他内部服务。
例如：
这里的
getPost
可以是服务端封装的数据访问函数，不必对应一个专门供浏览器调用的 HTTP API。
服务器完成组件执行后，向客户端发送渲染结果，而不需要将这段数据访问逻辑或整个组件的实现代码发送到浏览器。
在这种模式下，浏览器接收到的是 React 服务端渲染体系产生的结果，而不是必须自行消费一份 GraphQL JSON，再通过相应组件将其转换成界面。
变化的关键不只是少了一次 HTTP 请求，而是部分数据获取与消费过程被转移到了服务器内部。
如果应用服务器能够直接访问数据库，那么浏览器与数据库之间原本专门提供业务数据的 REST 或 GraphQL API，确实可能不再必要。
但这只适用于特定的架构条件。如果 React 服务器与实际业务后端是独立部署的系统，或者数据来自不同公司的服务，RSC 仍然需要通过相应的网络 API 获取数据。
因此，更准确的描述是：
RSC 可以让部分面向浏览器 UI 的数据 API 变得不再必要，但不会消除服务器之间的数据访问接口，也不会使 GraphQL 或 REST 失去独立价值。
三、RSC 与 Relay：两种不同的数据依赖组织方式
第二章讨论过 Relay 的 Fragment colocation。
Relay 的设计是让组件声明自己需要的数据，然后通过 GraphQL Fragment 和编译器，将这些声明组合为可执行查询。它解决的主要问题，是客户端组件的数据依赖如何被组织、复用和统一管理。
RSC 同样支持一种组件级的数据组织方式，但其实现逻辑不同：一个 Server Component 可以直接调用数据访问函数，并且可以将该函数放在组件附近。
例如，帖子组件获取帖子，评论组件获取评论，作者组件获取作者信息。
这些组件直接执行服务端函数。不再需要通过 GraphQL Fragment 声明数据需求，不再需要编译器将整棵组件树的数据需求组合为统一查询。
因此，Relay 和 RSC 在某些工程目标上存在重叠：
它们都希望组件拥有清晰的数据依赖，减少上层组件集中管理所有数据需求的负担：
Relay 通过静态 GraphQL 声明、编译器和客户端运行时协调数据依赖；
RSC 则让组件本身拥有服务端执行能力，可以在执行过程中直接获取数据。
这也带来了一个需要重视的差别。
Relay Compiler 可以分析静态声明的 GraphQL Fragment，生成查询结构并检查其是否符合 Schema。
RSC 不要求通过统一的 GraphQL Schema 来声明这些依赖。组件可以调用任意服务端数据函数，具体的查询优化与类型检查取决于所使用的数据访问层和工程工具。
RSC 减少了对客户端 GraphQL 数据查询层的依赖，但不自动提供 Relay 的全部编译期数据依赖分析和缓存管理能力。
同样，Relay 也并不因为 RSC 的出现而失去价值。
对于仍然需要在浏览器执行大量业务逻辑、持续获取和更新服务器数据的应用，Relay 的客户端缓存、Fragment 订阅、分页和数据更新机制仍然有适用场景。
两种技术的差异，首先来自组件在哪里执行，以及数据由谁获取和维护。
四、服务端组件并不会自动解决 N+1 与缓存问题
RSC 使组件能够直接访问服务端数据，但这并不意味着数据库查询天然高效。
如果一个帖子列表包含 20 个帖子组件，每个组件又分别加载作者信息，仍然可能发生大量重复数据库访问。
这种问题与第四章讨论的 GraphQL Resolver N+1，在底层原因上具有相似性：多个独立的数据需求没有得到有效的合并与复用。
RSC 不能仅凭组件在服务器执行，就自动将所有查询优化为一次数据库访问。服务端仍然需要采用批量查询、数据预加载、JOIN、请求级缓存或其他访问优化手段。
React 和 Next.js 为此提供了部分辅助机制：React 的
cache
可以在一次服务端请求的生命周期内复用某个数据函数的执行结果。Next.js 也提供针对数据获取的缓存和去重能力，以及对不同数据进行缓存与重新验证的机制。
但这里需要区分三个问题：
请求去重不等于批量加载
。对同一个用户重复调用相同的数据函数，可以通过请求级缓存避免重复执行。但查询 20 个不同用户时，仅仅进行请求去重并不能自动把 20 次数据库查询合并为一次。
数据缓存不等于缓存一致性
。当用户更新头像、修改帖子或新增评论后，哪些缓存应该失效、哪些组件应该更新，仍然需要相应的策略。
服务端缓存不等于客户端规范化缓存
。RSC 的服务器缓存主要关注数据获取和渲染结果的复用。Relay 和 Apollo 的规范化缓存，则主要关注浏览器中多个组件及查询对同一业务实体的共享、订阅和更新。
它们的实现层次与目标并不完全相同。
因此，
RSC 改变了部分缓存问题发生的位置，却没有消除缓存、数据加载和一致性管理本身的复杂度。
这也是不能把 RSC 理解为一套完整后端数据基础设施的重要原因。
五、GraphQL
@defer
@stream
与 React Suspense：数据的增量交付与界面的渐进渲染
在复杂应用中，不同数据的获取时间可能存在很大差异。如果必须等所有数据准备完毕才能显示页面，就可能让部分已经准备好的内容也被迫等待。
例如，一个 Facebook 帖子页面包含帖子正文和相关推荐。帖子正文只需要 100 毫秒就能获取，而相关推荐由于涉及额外的计算和数据查询，需要 2 秒才能返回。
如果客户端通过一个普通的 GraphQL 查询同时请求这两部分数据，服务器通常需要等整个查询执行完毕，才能返回完整结果。即使正文早已准备好，客户端也可能直到 2 秒后才获得数据。
一种解决方式是将请求拆开，让帖子正文和相关推荐分别加载。这在 REST 和 GraphQL 中都可以实现。
另一种方式则是：
在同一次查询中，允许服务器先返回已经准备好的数据，再逐步交付其余结果。
GraphQL 的
@defer
和
@stream
，就是围绕这种增量交付需求设计的机制。
1. GraphQL
@defer
：允许查询结果分批返回
@defer
是 GraphQL 的增量交付指令，用于将查询中的某部分数据延后返回，而不必等待整个查询完成。
例如，客户端可以声明需要帖子正文和相关推荐，但将相关推荐部分标记为延迟交付：
在服务端和客户端都支持增量交付的情况下，执行过程可以是：
首先，服务器获取帖子标题和正文，在约 100 毫秒后向客户端交付这些数据。
随后，服务器继续处理相关推荐。等这部分数据在约 2 秒后准备完成，再通过同一次查询的增量响应交付给客户端。
客户端不必等到全部数据准备好，便可以先使用已经收到的帖子内容。
这里的关键是，
@defer
控制的是 GraphQL 查询结果的交付过程，而不是 React 组件的渲染过程。
它允许数据分批到达，但并不直接规定界面应该如何显示这些数据。
2. GraphQL
@stream
：让列表数据逐步返回
@stream
也是一种增量交付指令，但主要针对列表。
例如，一个帖子有 100 条评论。如果客户端需要显示评论列表，服务器不一定要等全部评论准备完成后再一次性返回。
客户端可以指定先交付一部分评论：
在支持该机制的实现中，服务器可以先交付前 3 条评论，再逐步交付剩余评论。
因此，
@defer
和
@stream
的主要区别是：
@defer
：将查询中的某个数据片段延后交付。
@stream
：将列表中的元素分批交付。
两者都属于 GraphQL 数据层的增量交付能力。
需要注意，GraphQL 增量交付相关规范及不同实现的支持情况仍存在差异。不能假设所有 GraphQL 服务端、客户端和网络传输方案都已支持这些指令。
3. React Suspense：异步数据尚未准备好时，组件如何渲染？
GraphQL 的增量交付解决了数据如何分批返回的问题，但客户端收到部分数据后，界面应该怎样处理？
例如，帖子正文已经返回，相关推荐仍在加载。
我们希望页面先显示帖子正文，同时在相关推荐区域显示加载状态，等相关推荐准备好后再更新对应的组件。
React 的 Suspense 可以用于协调这种渲染行为。
例如：

相关推荐加载中...

}>
如果
Recommendations
组件依赖的异步资源尚未准备好，并且所使用的数据获取机制支持 Suspense，React 就可以暂时显示
fallback
中的内容。
等相关数据准备好，React 再渲染实际的相关推荐组件。
因此，
Suspense 关注的是组件在等待异步依赖时，应该如何协调渲染。
它并不负责向 GraphQL 服务器发出
@defer
指令，也不会让普通的异步请求自动变成增量数据响应。两者属于不同的技术层次：
GraphQL 控制数据怎样返回，React Suspense 控制依赖这些数据的组件怎样呈现。
它们也可以配合使用。例如，Relay 可以接收 GraphQL
@defer
逐步交付的数据，将其写入客户端 Store。相关 React 组件通过 Relay 读取数据，并利用 Suspense 处理数据尚未可用的状态。
这样，数据的增量交付与组件的渐进呈现就能够形成协作。
4. React Streaming：服务器渲染结果也可以逐步交付
前面讨论的是 GraphQL 查询结果分批返回，以及 React 组件如何等待数据。
如果页面本身在服务器渲染，还涉及另一个问题：服务器是否必须等整个页面渲染完成，才能向浏览器发送 HTML？
React 的 Streaming SSR（Streaming Server-Side Rendering，流式服务端渲染）允许服务器先发送已经完成的 HTML，再逐步发送其他部分的渲染结果。
例如，帖子正文已经完成渲染，而相关推荐组件仍在等待数据。
服务器可以先将帖子正文及相关推荐区域的加载状态交付给浏览器，随后再发送相关推荐的实际渲染结果。
因此，React Streaming 与 GraphQL 增量交付虽然都能够让客户端逐步收到内容，但交付的对象不同：
GraphQL 增量交付的是查询数据；React Streaming SSR 增量交付的是服务端渲染的页面内容。
两者可以独立使用，也可以在适当的架构中协同工作。
5. RSC 与这些机制又是什么关系？
React Server Components（RSC，React 服务器组件）进一步允许部分 React 组件直接在服务器执行，并访问服务端数据层。
在 RSC 架构中，帖子正文组件和相关推荐组件都可以作为服务器组件，分别获取所需数据。
React 可以结合 Suspense 和流式交付机制，先向客户端提供已经完成的部分，再交付其他服务器组件的结果。
此时，客户端逐步接收的可以是 React Server Component Payload（React 服务器组件载荷），而不一定是 GraphQL 查询返回的业务数据。
这里需要区分：
RSC 决定组件可以在哪里执行；Suspense 协调异步渲染；Streaming 则涉及渲染结果如何逐步传输。
这些不是同一种机制。传统 SSR 也可以使用 Suspense 和流式渲染，并不要求采用 RSC。
RSC 的重要变化在于，服务器组件可以直接消费数据，并生成相应的渲染结果。对于这类组件，浏览器不一定需要先通过 GraphQL 或 REST 获取业务数据，再自行渲染。
但如果服务器组件依然需要调用一个独立的 GraphQL 服务，它同样可以使用 GraphQL。RSC 并没有消除对数据查询接口的全部需求。
6. 这些技术并不具有简单的替代关系
综合来看，可以将几项技术的职责区分如下：

列表元素能否逐步交付
组件等待异步依赖时如何呈现
服务端生成的 HTML 如何逐步发送
哪些组件能够在服务器执行，以及服务器组件结果如何交付客户端

text.text: GraphQL 的增量交付与 React 的流式渲染，在最终用户体验上可能产生相似效果：页面不必等待所有内容准备完毕，就能逐步显示。
但它们解决的问题并不处于同一层次。
此外，让不同部分的页面先后显示，也并不是 GraphQL 或 RSC 独有的能力。
例如，使用 REST API 的客户端可以分别请求帖子正文和相关推荐。两次请求并行执行，正文数据先返回，React 就可以先显示正文，相关推荐随后更新。
因此，不能仅仅因为 GraphQL 支持增量交付，就认为它比 REST 天然具有更先进的渐进渲染能力；也不能因为 RSC 支持流式交付，就认为它直接取代了 GraphQL 的
@defer
和
@stream
GraphQL 的特点，是能够在同一套结构化查询中描述增量数据需求；React 的特点，是能够根据异步依赖协调组件渲染；RSC 则进一步改变了组件执行和数据消费的位置。
这三者既有协同空间，也分别具有独立的技术价值。
六、BFF、tRPC、oRPC：GraphQL 不是改善 API 协作的唯一选择
GraphQL 的重要价值之一，是让客户端能够根据自身需求获取数据，同时通过统一的 Schema 建立前后端之间的类型契约。
但这些需求并不只能通过 GraphQL 实现。
随着全栈开发框架、TypeScript 生态和 API 工具的发展，开发者已经拥有更多方式来组织前后端的数据交互。其中，BFF、tRPC 和 oRPC 分别代表了不同的解决思路。
需要注意，它们并不是三个与 GraphQL 处于同一层次的竞争产品。BFF 是一种应用架构模式，而 tRPC、oRPC 则主要是构建类型化 API 的开发工具。
1. BFF：由服务端适配不同客户端的数据需求
BFF（Backend for Frontend，面向前端的后端）是一种为特定客户端提供专用后端接口的架构模式。
假设一家公司的 Web、iOS 和 Android 客户端都需要展示帖子信息，但它们所需的数据结构并不相同。
传统做法可能是提供多个底层业务 API，由客户端自行请求帖子、作者和评论，再组织成需要的数据结构。
BFF 则可以在客户端与底层业务服务之间增加一层专门的服务。
例如，Web BFF 可以一次聚合帖子、作者和相关推荐的数据，再返回 Web 页面需要的结果。移动端 BFF 则可以根据移动应用的界面需求，提供不同的数据结构。
这样，客户端不必了解底层多个业务服务的具体组织方式，也能够减少自行组合数据的工作。
GraphQL 同样可以帮助客户端获取相互关联的数据，但二者的方式有所不同。
BFF 通常由服务端预先设计面向某类客户端的接口；GraphQL 则允许客户端在 Schema 所定义的范围内，自行选择和组合字段。
前者将数据适配逻辑更多地放在服务端，后者赋予客户端更大的查询灵活性。
但 BFF 和 GraphQL 并不互斥。BFF 完全可以对外提供 GraphQL API。
因此，BFF 并不是 GraphQL 的直接替代品，而是说明：针对客户端需求组织数据、减少客户端聚合工作，并不一定需要引入 GraphQL。
2. tRPC：通过 TypeScript 实现端到端类型安全
tRPC（TypeScript Remote Procedure Call）采用了不同的思路。
GraphQL 通过独立的 Schema 定义 API 类型，客户端根据 Schema 编写查询，并可以借助工具生成类型信息。
tRPC 则利用 TypeScript 的类型推导能力，让客户端直接获得服务端 API 的类型信息。
例如，服务端定义一个获取帖子详情的过程：
getPost({ id: 100 })
客户端调用该过程时，开发工具可以根据服务端定义推导参数和返回值的类型，而不必另外维护一套 GraphQL Schema。
这种方式特别适合前后端都采用 TypeScript，并且由同一团队或紧密协作的团队维护的应用。
不过，tRPC 的接口组织方式更接近 RPC（Remote Procedure Call，远程过程调用）。
客户端调用的是服务端已经定义好的过程，而不是像 GraphQL 那样，在统一的类型系统中自由选择字段及其关联关系。
例如，客户端调用
getPost
时，通常由服务端过程决定返回哪些数据。如果需要另一种数据组合，可以修改过程，或者设计其他过程。
GraphQL 则允许不同客户端通过不同查询，从同一套 Schema 中选择各自需要的字段。
这不是简单的优劣关系，而是两种不同的 API 契约设计。
tRPC 强调通过共享 TypeScript 类型降低开发协作成本；GraphQL 则通过独立于编程语言的 Schema 和查询语言，提供可组合的数据访问接口。
3. oRPC：类型化 RPC 与标准化 API 描述
oRPC 也以 TypeScript 为基础，提供类型化远程过程调用能力，并支持运行时输入验证，以及与 OpenAPI 的集成。
OpenAPI（OpenAPI Specification，开放 API 规范）用于以机器可读的方式描述 HTTP API，包括接口路径、参数、请求和响应结构等。
这意味着，开发者可以在使用类型推导改善 TypeScript 开发体验的同时，通过 OpenAPI 描述接口，支持文档生成以及其他语言客户端的工具化接入。
oRPC 与 GraphQL 的差别仍然在于 API 的基本抽象。
oRPC 主要围绕服务端定义的过程及其输入、输出类型组织接口。
GraphQL 则提供一套面向数据对象及其关联关系的查询语言，允许客户端自行决定所需字段。
因此，oRPC 展示的是另一种技术组合：不采用 GraphQL Schema，也可以建立类型化、可验证、具有标准化接口描述能力的 API。
但 OpenAPI 所提供的接口描述，并不等同于 GraphQL 的字段选择和关联查询机制。
4. GraphQL 的竞争优势究竟在哪里？
BFF、tRPC 和 oRPC 的发展，说明 GraphQL 曾经受到重视的部分能力，如今已经有多种实现方式。
减少客户端请求数量，可以通过 BFF 聚合接口实现。
前后端类型安全，可以通过 TypeScript 类型推导、OpenAPI 和代码生成工具实现。
客户端不再手动组合多个底层服务的数据，也可以通过专门设计的 REST 或 RPC 接口实现。
以上这些能力都不应被当作 GraphQL 独有的优势。
GraphQL 更具有辨识度的设计，是将统一的类型化数据模型，与客户端可自行编写的结构化查询结合起来。
这使客户端能够在服务器提供的 Schema 范围内，选择字段、访问关联对象，并利用 Fragment 等机制组织可复用的数据需求。但这种查询自由度也带来了执行成本、权限控制、缓存和 Schema 治理等额外要求。
因此，选择 GraphQL 还是其他 API 方案，不只是比较谁能提供类型安全或减少 HTTP 请求，更需要判断：
应用是否真正需要一套由客户端灵活组合数据的查询接口，以及这种灵活性是否值得相应的工程成本。
七、GraphQL 在现代 Web 架构中的新位置
从传统客户端渲染到 RSC，再到 BFF 和类型化 RPC 的发展，可以看到，GraphQL 当初试图解决的许多问题，如今已经有了不同的技术路径。
这些变化并不意味着 GraphQL 正在被某一种技术完整取代，而是让它在不同应用架构中的必要性产生了差异。
对于以前后端紧密集成为特点的全栈 React 应用，Server Components 可以直接调用服务端数据函数。如果应用的数据需求相对简单，或者业务接口主要服务于单一 Web 客户端，那么建立额外的 GraphQL 查询层，可能并不能带来足够收益。
对于使用 TypeScript 的前后端一体化项目，tRPC、oRPC 等工具也可能以更直接的方式满足类型安全与 API 协作需求。
但在复杂的客户端应用中，GraphQL 仍然可以通过结构化查询、Fragment 组合及 Relay 等数据管理工具，为组件之间的数据依赖协作提供支持。
而在需要同时服务 Web、移动端、第三方应用和多个业务系统的架构中，GraphQL 也可以继续作为独立于具体 UI 框架的查询接口。
不过，拥有多个客户端并不自动意味着应该使用 GraphQL。其价值仍然取决于不同客户端是否真正需要灵活的数据选择与组合，以及统一 Schema 能否降低长期协作成本。
由此可以将 GraphQL 在现代应用中的角色概括为三种：

cells.text: 复杂的客户端 Web 应用
浏览器数据查询接口，与 Relay、Apollo 等工具配合
以 RSC 为主的全栈 React 应用
可选的服务端数据查询层，也可能被直接服务端函数调用取代
多客户端、复杂业务数据平台
跨客户端的统一查询契约，支持不同数据需求的组合

text.text: 这三类场景并不是严格互斥的。同一个系统也可能同时使用 RSC、GraphQL、REST 和 RPC，由它们分别承担不同职责。
因此，现代 Web 架构带来的变化，不是让 GraphQL 从技术上变得过时，而是使它不再需要承担某些原本由客户端 API 负责的数据获取任务。
GraphQL 的价值需要回到具体应用架构中判断：它所提供的统一 Schema、结构化查询和可组合数据契约，能否创造超过其执行、维护与治理成本的实际收益。
这也为最后一章重新评价 GraphQL 的优势、局限与适用条件提供了基础。

events.title: 重新理解 GraphQL - 04：从 Facebook 到行业实践——GraphQL 为什么容易走样？
events.subtitle: 从 Facebook 的设计哲学到现实中的工程困境

en.title: Rethinking GraphQL - 04: From Facebook to Industry Adoption—Why Does GraphQL So Often Lose Its Way?
en.subtitle: From Facebook’s design philosophy to the engineering challenges of real-world adoption

text.text: How did GraphQL’s ideas change as adoption grew after it was open-sourced?
Differences between Apollo and Relay in design philosophy, engineering constraints, and practice.
Why do some teams simply replace REST with GraphQL?
Why might the frontend miss out on component-level data management benefits?
The backend costs of resolvers, N+1 queries, ASTs, query complexity, and cache management.
Do these problems come from GraphQL’s design or from unsuitable engineering practices?
This chapter asks why some teams gain fewer frontend benefits than expected while ending up with a more complex backend.
The first three chapters examined GraphQL’s original design, Relay’s frontend data management system, and Facebook’s backend data infrastructure.
These technologies do not form an indivisible architecture. GraphQL can be used independently, Relay is not the only client option, and servers do not need infrastructure on Facebook’s scale.

As GraphQL moved from an internal Facebook technology to a general-purpose API technology, however, a recurring pattern emerged: teams introduced GraphQL without changing how the frontend managed data dependencies or fully considering the complexities of backend execution, caching, and authorization.
In that situation, GraphQL may add another architectural layer to maintain without delivering enough additional benefit.
This chapter examines why that pattern occurs and distinguishes problems arising from GraphQL’s design from those arising from particular implementations.
1. From an Engineering System to a General API: Adoption Patterns Changed
GraphQL originated in Facebook’s mobile development environment and gradually came to work with internal data services and technologies such as React and Relay.
After it was open-sourced, other companies adopted it in very different engineering environments.

Most teams already had REST APIs, relational databases, ORMs, caches, and existing business logic. Adopting GraphQL generally meant adding a new API layer to those systems, rather than redesigning the entire application architecture.
A typical structure looks like this:

React / Vue and other clients
         ↓
   Apollo Client
         ↓
   GraphQL Server
         ↓
      Resolvers
         ↓
Existing REST services / ORM / database
GraphQL primarily serves as a data-querying interface in this architecture.
There is nothing inherently wrong with that. GraphQL has emphasized independence from underlying storage from the beginning, allowing it to sit on top of existing business systems.
But this can lead to two different implementations:
One uses GraphQL as a new application data abstraction, reorganizing client data requirements and server-side loading mechanisms.
The other largely retains the existing architecture, wraps REST endpoints as GraphQL fields, and lets clients access them through GraphQL queries.
The latter can provide a more unified schema, query composition, and typed interfaces, without fundamentally improving how data is organized:

If the application already suffers from tangled page-level dependencies, duplicate requests, inefficient database queries, or poor caching, adding GraphQL does not automatically make those problems disappear.

It may even add maintenance work. The original REST API still needs support, as do the GraphQL schema and resolvers, together with the mappings between their data models, error handling, and authorization rules.
This is not an inevitable outcome of GraphQL. It is an architectural choice whose costs should be assessed before adoption.
Moving from REST to GraphQL can involve at least two distinct goals:
Changing how the API expresses data access.
Improving the application’s overall data management architecture.
2. The Frontend: Using GraphQL Does Not Automatically Provide Declarative Dependency Management
Chapter 2 examined Relay’s core approach: components declare data requirements through fragments, while a compiler and runtime coordinate querying, caching, and rendering.
GraphQL does not require developers to adopt that approach.
A React page can simply use Apollo Client’s useQuery, define a complete query at the page level, and pass its results to child components as props.

This resembles page-level fetching in a conventional REST application. It is simple and direct, and gives the page centralized control of requests and loading states. In a large application with many frequently reused components, however, data dependencies may remain coupled to individual pages.
Suppose several pages reuse a user information component. If each page lists the fields that component needs in its own query, changing the component’s requirements may require updating every page.
GraphQL lets clients choose fields, but does not require components to declare those fields themselves or automatically keep page queries aligned with actual component dependencies.
Client-side field selection is therefore different from independent data dependency boundaries for components.
GraphQL introductions can easily overlook this distinction.
The first is a query-language capability. The second requires additional practices such as fragment colocation, type checking, and data masking.
A team may reduce network requests for some pages using GraphQL while continuing to maintain the same coupling between pages and components.
GraphQL is then providing some of its potential benefits, rather than none at all.

The reverse also matters: not using fragment colocation does not necessarily indicate poor design. Centralized queries can be easier to understand and maintain for small projects, stable page structures, or components that are rarely reused.
The value of fragment colocation depends on project size, component reuse, team responsibilities, and data-model complexity. It is not a universal requirement for every project.
3. Apollo and Relay: The Difference Is Not Whether They Have Fragments or Caching
Apollo Client and Relay are frequently compared in frontend GraphQL discussions.
A common but inaccurate claim is that only Relay offers fragment colocation and normalized caching, while Apollo merely sends GraphQL requests.
That does not reflect modern Apollo Client. Apollo also supports fragment colocation, normalized caching, useFragment, data masking, and type generation through tools such as GraphQL Code Generator.
Its official documentation explains fragment colocation and explicitly recommends composing direct children’s fragments in their parent component to reduce coupling.
Apollo’s useFragment can also subscribe a component to specific cached data, instead of tying it to changes in the entire page query result.
The fact that some teams use only useQuery does not describe Apollo’s full capabilities.
An important difference between Relay and Apollo is the strength of their engineering constraints and their default organizational models.

Relay emphasizes an integrated approach: components declare requirements through fragments, queries and fragments go through a compiler, fragment boundaries constrain data access, and the runtime manages reads and updates around those conventions.
This reduces the range of approaches teams can choose, but can provide more consistent practices for large projects.
Apollo offers more flexible client-side data management. Developers can choose query, fragment, caching, and state-management patterns to suit their project.

With fragment colocation, data masking, code generation, and sound caching policies, Apollo can also support clear component dependency boundaries. Teams using only basic queries without corresponding component data conventions may leave those capabilities underused.
A more accurate assessment is:
Relay puts a relatively strong set of engineering constraints at the center of its framework design, while Apollo gives teams more choice in organizing data management.
The former involves learning costs, a compilation toolchain, and engineering constraints. The latter may require teams to establish and maintain more conventions themselves.
Neither is universally better independently of project conditions.
The useful questions are why Facebook chose Relay’s more constrained design, and whether other teams have sufficient scale and complexity to benefit similarly.
4. The Backend: One GraphQL Request Does Not Mean One Data Access Operation

One easily understood frontend advantage of GraphQL is retrieving several related objects in a single network request. That benefit applies at the client–GraphQL-server boundary; it makes no equivalent guarantee about data access inside the server.
Suppose a page displays 20 posts, each with its author and latest comments.
The client can send one GraphQL query declaring the post, author, and comment fields.
A straightforward backend implementation might:
Query the database once to retrieve 20 posts.
Query each post’s author separately, producing 20 database queries.
Query each post’s comments separately, producing another 20 database queries.
The client sends one GraphQL request, but the database may execute 41 queries.
These numbers illustrate an execution pattern, not a fixed overhead imposed by GraphQL.
With batching, the backend could fetch the 20 posts and then load their authors and comments in batches, reducing the number of database queries.
Appropriate joins, eager loading, materialized results, or specialized data services may also improve execution.
The query’s GraphQL structure does not automatically determine which optimizations should be applied.
GraphQL allows relatively independent resolvers for individual fields. This helps schemas evolve, but independently fetching data in each resolver can readily produce N+1 queries.
N+1 is not unique to GraphQL. REST services using ORMs can encounter it too.

GraphQL clients can, however, combine related fields flexibly, exposing the server to more possible query shapes. An optimized query written for one fixed REST endpoint may not cover every GraphQL combination.
That is why DataLoader, request-scoped caching, batching, and data access layer design matter so much in GraphQL servers.

One technical point needs clarification: GraphQL performance problems cannot simply be blamed on AST parsing. Servers parse query text into an abstract syntax tree, validate it, and resolve fields according to execution rules. Those operations have costs, but in business queries involving many database or cross-service calls, the bottleneck is often data retrieval rather than AST parsing itself.

Optimizing parsing, using precompiled documents, or adopting persisted queries can reduce some overhead. They will not resolve the overall problem if execution still performs large amounts of inefficient data access.
Query parsing, field execution, and underlying database or service access therefore need to be distinguished.
5. Query Flexibility Versus Server-Side Cost Control
Another GraphQL challenge is that clients can construct queries with widely varying complexity.
With APIs that return fixed response structures, a server can generally predict an endpoint’s main data access operations more easily.
GraphQL lets clients combine fields and nested relationships within the schema and use arguments to control how much data is returned.
A query might retrieve a user’s friends, each friend’s posts, and each post’s comments.
If every collection can contain many objects, the result size can grow rapidly with nesting depth.
Not every nested GraphQL query has exponential cost, but servers cannot judge query cost simply by counting HTTP requests.
Reading one user’s name and reading thousands of related objects and their attributes each take one request, yet consume very different amounts of resources.
Production GraphQL services therefore usually need several controls:
Depth limits constrain nesting, but shallow queries are not necessarily cheap. Even two or three levels can consume substantial resources if some fields return enormous collections.
Complexity analysis assigns costs using fields, arguments, and expected result sizes. Expensive fields can have stricter rules.
Pagination and result-size limits prevent uncontrolled retrieval of large relationship collections in one request.
Timeouts, rate limits, and concurrency controls stop expensive queries from continually monopolizing compute and database resources.

Some internal applications also use trusted documents or query allowlists. In addition to limits on depth, complexity, and result size, servers restrict which queries clients may execute. Developers register the application’s required queries in advance, and the server rejects other ad hoc queries. This prevents arbitrary new query structures, but registered queries can still be expensive. Argument limits, complexity analysis, and rate limiting remain necessary.
GraphQL’s flexibility therefore has a cost. The more freely clients can compose requirements, the more comprehensive the server’s query-cost and execution controls must be.
6. Caching: Client-Side Benefits and Server-Side Costs
Caching is a particularly common source of misunderstanding in GraphQL–REST comparisons.
Combined with Relay or Apollo Client, GraphQL can support normalized caches that let components share entity data and coordinate updates.
HTTP/CDN caching, on the other hand, often needs more design work than ordinary REST resource endpoints.
These are completely different caching layers.
6.1 Client-Side Caching: Why Does GraphQL Fit Normalized Caches?
Suppose the same user appears in Facebook’s home feed, on a profile page, and in a friends list.
All three need the user’s name and avatar. Saving complete query results separately may produce three copies of the same user data.
When the user changes their avatar, all those copies may need updating.
Relay Store and Apollo Client’s InMemoryCache address this by using object identifiers to organize the same entity returned by different queries as one shared cache record.
If three queries return user ID 123, the client cache can recognize that they refer to the same user.
When the avatar in that record changes, other components depending on it can receive update notifications.
This mechanism is called a normalized cache.
Its value includes both reducing duplicate data and making shared entity data easier to update across components.

Normalized caching is not automatically provided by the GraphQL language. It is implemented by client frameworks such as Relay and Apollo, and depends on stable object identity and suitable cache policies.
REST clients can implement normalization too, but GraphQL’s typed schema, object field selection, and fragment composition provide a suitable foundation.
6.2 HTTP/CDN Caching: Why Is REST Usually More Direct?
Client-side normalization addresses how data is managed inside the browser.
HTTP/CDN caching addresses a different question: when users request the same data, can a previous response be reused without reaching the application server again?
For example, a client might request a post through REST:
GET /posts/100
The server can use HTTP headers such as Cache-Control to specify how long the response may be cached.
When caching conditions permit, a CDN can store the response for /posts/100. Later requests for that resource may receive the cached response without reaching the application server.
This is relatively direct because the URL is an important part of distinguishing cache entries: different posts generally have different URLs.
A common GraphQL request pattern differs. Clients submit POST requests to the same address, even though their contents can be completely different.
POST /graphql
One client may request the title of post 100, while another requests the author and comments of post 200.
Both requests go to /graphql, but require different responses.

Conventional CDNs mainly provide ordinary shared caching for methods such as GET and HEAD. They do not usually inspect GraphQL POST bodies automatically and cache responses separately according to their queries.
Using HTTP/CDN caching effectively with GraphQL therefore usually requires additional decisions about request identity.
6.3 What Must GraphQL HTTP/CDN Caching Address?
There are three main concerns.
First, cache-key design.
The cache key determines whether two requests can reuse the same result.
For a simple REST resource API, GET /posts/100 and GET /posts/200 can generally be distinguished by URL. Different GraphQL requests may all use the same /graphql address.
The cache therefore needs to distinguish query contents and variables.
Requesting post 100’s title and requesting its title plus comments concern the same post, but do not produce interchangeable responses.
One solution is to send read-only GraphQL queries with GET, encoding the query and variables in the URL so a CDN can distinguish results using the complete request address.
A GraphQL server or cache gateway can also generate dedicated keys from query contents and variables.
Second, user identity and authorization.
Suppose a query requests a post together with whether the current user has liked it.
The like status for that post might be true for user A and false for user B.
Even if they submit identical GraphQL queries, they cannot simply share a complete response containing personal like status.
Incorrect sharing of private profile data or friends-only content could even expose confidential information.
Cache policies must therefore distinguish responses that can be shared publicly, responses requiring identity or permission isolation, and responses that must not enter a public CDN cache.
REST APIs requiring authentication and authorization face the same issue. It is not exclusive to GraphQL.
Finally, cache invalidation.
Suppose a GraphQL query returns:

Post 100
 ├── Title
 ├── Author name
 └── Latest 10 comments
The server or CDN caches that result.
The author then changes their name. Post 100 has not changed, but the author name in the response is stale.
Adding or removing a comment may also require updating this cache entry.
The system must decide how changes to users, posts, or comments affect cached queries containing them.
A simple approach is to use a short expiry period and fetch fresh data afterward.
A more sophisticated approach tracks which entities a result depends on, then removes affected entries through cache tags or invalidation notifications when those entities change.
The latter permits more precise management, but requires maintaining relationships between entities and cached results.
GraphQL’s flexible field selection and relationship composition let different queries return overlapping data, potentially making dependencies complex when precise invalidation is required.
This is not unique to GraphQL either. A REST aggregation endpoint returning authors, posts, and comments also needs invalidation when related data changes.
6.4 Distinguishing Client, Server, and CDN Caches
The preceding discussion concerns three layers.

cells.text: Sharing data and coordinating updates between components
Reducing repeated computation and underlying database access
Request-scoped caching, DataLoader, Redis, TAO, and similar systems
Reusing responses directly to reduce application-server traffic
Browser HTTP caches, CDNs, response caches

text.text: The three can work together, but cannot replace one another.
Relay Store manages sharing between components in one browser. It does not automatically reduce database load from other users reaching Facebook’s servers.
TAO efficiently caches Facebook’s social graph objects and associations, but does not manage subscriptions and updates for React components in the browser.
A CDN reduces HTTP traffic when requests hit its cache, but does not automatically keep every entity in the client’s normalized cache consistent.
Facebook’s Relay and TAO both provide caching, but address different client-side and server-side layers.
6.5 Is GraphQL Caching an Advantage or a Disadvantage?
It is too simplistic to claim GraphQL caching is better than REST, or that its common use of POST prevents effective CDN caching.
On the client, typed queries and object relationships work well with normalization and fragment subscriptions to help complex applications manage shared data.

At the HTTP/CDN layer, conventional REST GET endpoints are usually easier to cache with existing mechanisms. GraphQL can also use GET queries, response caching, and suitable configuration, but policies must account for query contents, variables, and permissions.

On the server, both must address database access, repeated loading, and cache consistency. GraphQL’s flexibility can add execution and cache-management complexity, but REST can encounter similar problems.

Client-side caching benefits do not automatically translate into a system-wide caching advantage. Comparing GraphQL and REST performance requires considering client management, server-side access, and HTTP/CDN caching together, including maintenance costs.
7. Authorization and Schema Governance: The Other Side of a Flexible API

GraphQL uses a common schema to describe business objects, fields, and relationships available to clients. This improves frontend–backend collaboration and lets different clients develop against a shared data model.

Describing fields does not determine which users may access their data. And when multiple clients and teams share a schema, maintaining long-term interface stability becomes another engineering concern.
These concerns are authorization and schema governance, respectively.
7.1 A Valid Query Does Not Imply Authorized Access
Suppose a Facebook post has a title, body, draft status, and internal moderation notes.
Ordinary users may see its title and public body, only the author may see draft status, and only administrators may see internal moderation notes.
A GraphQL schema could define:

type Post {
  id: ID!
  title: String!
  content: String!
  draft: Boolean
  reviewNote: String
}
If an ordinary user requests title and reviewNote, GraphQL’s type validation will not automatically reject the query because the user lacks administrator permissions.
Schema validation checks conformance to type definitions: whether fields exist and arguments and types are valid. It does not determine whether the requester may access their contents.
The GraphQL server must implement authentication and business authorization separately.
It might allow title while denying reviewNote. Whether it returns an error or null depends on the schema and authorization behavior.
Authorization may apply to individual fields or entire business objects.
For a friends-only post, even a query requesting only a normally public field such as title must first establish whether the user may view that post.
7.2 Why Not Put Every Permission Check in Resolvers?
GraphQL allows checks inside resolvers, such as requiring administrator status before returning reviewNote.
That is valid, but independent checks in every resolver can produce duplication and security risks as applications grow.
The same private post may be reachable through profiles, friends’ feeds, and search results.
If each path implements permissions separately, one resolver may check visibility correctly while another omits the check.
A more reliable approach usually centralizes core authorization rules in business logic or an entity access layer, letting GraphQL resolvers and other API entry points reuse them.
Facebook’s internal Ent offers a useful example.
Beyond loading and caching entities, Ent is privacy-aware. Entity access can evaluate the requester’s identity together with the relevant business rules.
Authorization therefore need not depend entirely on independent resolver implementations.
Not every field permission must live in the entity layer. Some interface-, operation-, and field-specific permissions still belong elsewhere.

The central principle is that GraphQL’s type system cannot replace business authorization. Critical rules should be maintained in a common business layer wherever practical to prevent inconsistent decisions across access paths.
7.3 Schema Governance: Keeping Multiple Clients Compatible
Continuous schema evolution also creates management costs.
Suppose Facebook’s schema defines:
Web, iOS, and Android clients all use this schema.
The development team decides to rename title to headline.
Deleting title immediately and retaining only headline would cause query validation failures in clients still using the old field.
This is especially difficult with native mobile apps: releasing a new version does not guarantee that everyone upgrades immediately.
GraphQL provides field deprecation for this purpose:
The server can retain both fields temporarily, keeping old clients functional while newer clients migrate to headline.
This supports gradual evolution, but does not automatically solve every compatibility problem.
Changing a return type, adding a required argument, removing an enum value, or changing a field’s business meaning can all affect existing clients.
Marking a field deprecated does not mean it can be removed immediately. Teams still need to know which clients use it and whether they have migrated.
7.4 Why Do Large Organizations Need Dedicated Schema Governance?
When dozens of teams maintain one GraphQL schema, interface management involves more than editing type definitions.
The user team and social relationships team might both extend User. Another team may want to change a field’s meaning or remove an apparently unused field.
Clear rules are needed: who owns each type and field, whether additions require review, how to detect changes that break existing queries, and when deprecated fields can safely be removed.
GraphQL’s type system and query documents provide a technical foundation for this governance.
Comparing old and new schemas can identify potentially breaking changes. Retaining the query documents clients actually use allows checks of which operations would be affected.
These checks and management practices still require additional tooling and organizational processes. The language does not supply a complete governance system automatically.
The schema defines a common contract for multiple clients. Governance keeps that contract reliable and maintainable over time.
7.5 Why Not Convert Database Tables Directly into a GraphQL Schema?
Governance also raises a more fundamental question: how should the API’s public data model be designed?
GraphQL originally emphasized client requirements rather than exposing internal database structure directly.
A posts table might contain:

id
title
content
author_id
moderation_status
internal_review_note
database_shard_id
Here, author_id represents a database relationship, while database_shard_id may describe internal storage architecture.
Mechanically mapping every database field to GraphQL can expose unnecessary storage details and internal information.
A better approach is to define the API model around client business requirements:
The author field returns a user object directly, rather than requiring clients to understand author_id and query that user separately.
Internal shard identifiers need not appear in the public schema either.
Then, even if the database structure changes, clients need not change as long as business semantics and the schema remain stable.
Whether internal fields belong in a particular schema nevertheless depends on its audience and authorization model. A field sharing a database column’s name is not inherently bad design.
The key is that the schema should follow the business data contract, not be mechanically dictated by the database structure.
7.6 Engineering Requirements for Authorization and Governance
GraphQL combines business objects and relationships in a common schema and lets clients compose queries flexibly. This improves access but imposes clearer management requirements:

Authorization must distinguish the ability to construct a query from the right to access every datum it requests. Critical permissions must be enforced consistently at suitable business-logic or data-access layers.
Schema evolution must avoid casually breaking existing clients. APIs shared by multiple teams also need field ownership, compatibility checks, and change management.
Data modeling should avoid treating database tables as the public business contract, reducing coupling between clients and internal storage.
REST, RPC, and other APIs also need authorization, compatibility, and data modeling. These issues are not exclusive to GraphQL.
Its unified, typed, field-composable model nevertheless concentrates many of them in schema design, resolver execution, and governance of cross-client contracts.
GraphQL’s flexibility therefore increases not only execution and caching requirements, but also the importance of authorization and long-term schema maintenance in its engineering costs.
8. Compare Benefits and Costs at the Same Architectural Layer
GraphQL debates often compare unlike systems.
One example compares a complete GraphQL system with Relay, a compiler, normalized caching, and mature backend governance against unoptimized REST endpoints, attributing every advantage to GraphQL.
The reverse compares a poorly implemented GraphQL service with N+1 and caching problems against a carefully optimized REST/BFF architecture, attributing every problem to GraphQL.
Neither is persuasive. A better comparison separates the layers of capability.

cells.text: Schemas, field selection, nested queries, fragments
A language foundation for declarative composition
Batch loading, query planning, database optimization
Depth and complexity limits, pagination, rate limiting
HTTP caching, server caches, business authorization

text.text: Many practical GraphQL benefits do require complementary technologies to be fully realized.
Those technologies are not necessarily exclusive to GraphQL.
REST can use a BFF to aggregate underlying service data into page-specific responses, generate types through OpenAPI, and use a common client framework for caching and updates.
GraphQL’s fragment composition and typed queries have their own strengths, but not every component-management, asynchronous-request, or caching feature is unique to GraphQL.
The meaningful comparison asks which architecture produces better development efficiency, runtime performance, and maintainability under the same requirements and comparable engineering investment.
9. When Is GraphQL More Worthwhile?
Suitability depends on business characteristics, not how advanced a technology’s ideas sound.
GraphQL can be valuable for applications with multiple clients, frequently changing requirements, and complex relationships between business objects.
The gains are especially clear when clients compose the same data in different ways and a common schema, generated types, and fragment management improve collaboration.
For projects with many reusable UI components, component-level dependency management through Relay or Apollo may further reduce maintenance costs.
Conversely, REST, a BFF, or typed RPC may be more direct for a small set of fixed pages, stable interfaces, and a small team maintaining both frontend and backend.
Adding schemas, resolvers, client caches, and query-governance tools may not produce enough benefit there.
GraphQL’s best use cases are not limited to applications as large as Facebook.

Small and medium projects can benefit from multiple clients, complex composition, or strongly typed tooling. Some large systems, meanwhile, have mature APIs and stable query patterns that provide little reason to migrate.
Adoption should be assessed through concrete questions:
Do clients really repeat substantial data composition work?
Can GraphQL reduce interface maintenance and cross-team coordination?
Will the team use fragments and type tooling to manage dependencies?
Can the server execute permitted client queries efficiently?
How much must existing caching, authorization, and monitoring change?
These questions are more useful than comparing feature lists alone.
10. Do GraphQL’s Problems Come from the Technology or Its Use?
Why do some teams adopt GraphQL without obtaining the expected frontend benefits, while increasing backend complexity?
There are three levels to the answer.
First, adoption goals may not match the technology. If a team needs only a few fixed interfaces, adopting GraphQL for field selection and one endpoint may cost more on the server than it saves.

Second, teams may adopt the language without fully using complementary data management. They keep traditional page-level dependencies without systematically using fragments, compilation tools, or data isolation.

Finally, they may underestimate execution and governance. GraphQL allows flexible requirements but does not automatically provide efficient loading, cost controls, authorization, or cache consistency.
Those capabilities require additional investment and continuing maintenance.
That does not absolve the technology itself of every responsibility.
A language and execution model set capability boundaries and influence which engineering problems are likely to arise.
GraphQL’s flexible queries expose servers to more varied access patterns. The resolver model improves modularity while also making inefficient data access easy to implement.
These are architectural trade-offs, not problems that can all be dismissed as developer misuse.

Nor is there sufficient evidence that most GraphQL projects follow this failure pattern. Apollo and other ecosystem tools offer mature client data management, and industry practice includes substantial work on performance, caching, and governance.
A more accurate conclusion is:

GraphQL has genuine standalone value, but its benefits are not equivalent to Facebook’s complete engineering system. Adopting only the language may not deliver all the advantages of Relay-style dependency management and mature backend infrastructure. Obtaining those advantages also involves corresponding costs.
This does not make Facebook’s architecture a universal goal.

Its system serves particular scales, organizational structures, and products. Other companies may reasonably choose full Relay adoption, Apollo with suitable conventions, or REST, a BFF, and other API approaches.
We have now examined GraphQL’s origins, Facebook’s frontend and backend systems, and the engineering gaps that can appear in wider adoption.
Web architecture itself continues to change.

React Server Components let some components execute directly on the server, changing the relationship between browser fetching, server-side data organization, and rendering. Some problems previously addressed with client-side GraphQL or REST requests can consequently be handled through different architectures.
The next chapter examines this shift and how GraphQL’s role in modern web applications should be reassessed.
